A.feedback: New nucleotides are added to the 3′ end, so the strand grows 5′ to 3′.

B.feedback: Correct. DNA polymerase adds to the 3′ end, so synthesis runs 5′ to 3′.

A.feedback: Correct. DNA polymerase can only extend an existing complementary strand, and the primer provides that start.

B.feedback: Ligase joins pieces of DNA. It does not add the new bases. DNA polymerase extends a primer that primase made.

C.feedback: DNA is synthesized 5′ to 3′. The primer matters because polymerase needs an existing start to extend.

A.feedback: Correct. The primer's 3′ end is where polymerase adds the next nucleotide.

B.feedback: Polymerase adds to the 3′ end, never the 5′ end.

A.feedback: Primase makes the RNA primer. Unlike DNA polymerase, it can start from scratch on a single template strand.

B.feedback: Correct. Primase makes the RNA primer that DNA polymerase extends.

C.feedback: DNA polymerase can't start a strand on its own. Primase makes the primer first.

A.feedback: Correct. Nucleotides join at the 3′ end, so the strand grows 5′ to 3′.

B.feedback: The new strand grows 5′ to 3′ because nucleotides are added only at the 3′ end.

A.feedback: Primase makes the primer but doesn't extend it. DNA polymerase adds the DNA nucleotides.

B.feedback: Correct. Primase starts the strand with RNA, then DNA polymerase extends it.

C.feedback: Ligase closes gaps in the backbone without adding new bases. DNA polymerase extends the primer.

A.feedback: Mismatch repair happens after replication is complete, not immediately.

B.feedback: Correct. Polymerase backs up, removes the wrong base from the 3′ end, and adds the right one.

C.feedback: The wrong base is fixed right away by DNA polymerase's own exonuclease activity, not by ligase.

A.feedback: UV doesn't separate the strands. It bonds adjacent C's and T's together, creating a bulge.

B.feedback: UV doesn't change DNA into RNA. It bonds adjacent C's and T's, creating a bulge.

C.feedback: Correct. The bulge stops genes from being copied or transcribed normally.

A.feedback: Correct. Mismatch repair checks the finished double helix.

B.feedback: Mismatch repair checks new DNA, so it happens after replication.

C.feedback: Checking each base as it's added is proofreading. Mismatch repair comes after replication.

A.feedback: Bases are replaced only after the damaged section is found and cut out.

B.feedback: Correct. Repair starts by recognizing where the damage is.

C.feedback: Linking the backbone is the last step, after the bases are replaced.

A.feedback: Correct. Proofreading is done by DNA polymerase as it copies.

B.feedback: Mismatch repair happens after replication is complete. Proofreading happens during copying.

A.feedback: The helix is opened earlier, before the damaged bases are removed.

B.feedback: No primer is involved. The last step reseals the backbone with phosphodiester linkages.

C.feedback: Correct. Phosphodiester linkages reconnect the new bases to the adjacent DNA.

A.feedback: The coding strand is the one that is not transcribed. RNA polymerase reads the template strand.

B.feedback: Correct. The template strand is read and transcribed.

A.feedback: Correct. The promoter is where transcription starts, and it sets the reading direction.

B.feedback: Codons are only in translation. A promoter is a DNA region where transcription starts.

C.feedback: The promoter is part of the gene's DNA, not the RNA product.

A.feedback: The template strand is the one that is transcribed.

B.feedback: Correct. The coding strand is the complementary strand that isn't transcribed.

A.feedback: Amino acids are added during translation, not set by the promoter.

B.feedback: Correct. The promoter also sets the reading direction.

C.feedback: Ribosomes are part of translation. The promoter acts in transcription.

A.feedback: Correct. RNA is built to match the template strand that RNA polymerase reads.

B.feedback: RNA polymerase reads the template strand, so the RNA is complementary to it.

A.feedback: tRNAs act in translation, not at the promoter.

B.feedback: Ligase seals DNA backbone gaps. It doesn't start transcription.

C.feedback: Correct. Once the helix is unwound at the promoter, RNA polymerase can start.

A.feedback: The A site is where charged tRNAs enter. The peptide bond forms in the P site.

B.feedback: Correct. The bond forms between the amino acids held in the P and A sites.

C.feedback: The E site holds uncharged tRNAs on their way out.

A.feedback: Correct. UAC is complementary to AUG, and that tRNA carries methionine.

B.feedback: An anticodon is complementary to the codon, not identical to it.

C.feedback: CCA is the tRNA's amino-acid attachment site, not its anticodon.

A.feedback: The E site is where uncharged tRNAs exit.

B.feedback: Correct. Charged tRNAs enter at the A site.

C.feedback: The P site is where the peptide bond forms.

A.feedback: CCA is the attachment site. The anticodon is a different part of the tRNA.

B.feedback: The amino acid is the cargo. The anticodon is the three bases that read the codon.

C.feedback: Correct. The anticodon pairs with a matching codon in the mRNA.

A.feedback: The P site is where the peptide bond forms. The tRNA leaves from the E site.

B.feedback: The A site is where charged tRNAs enter.

C.feedback: Correct. After its amino acid is added, the tRNA exits from the E site.

A.feedback: Correct. It stays only if its anticodon pairs with the codon.

B.feedback: Only the start tRNA carries methionine. Any tRNA can stay if its anticodon matches.

C.feedback: tRNAs entering the A site are charged. Pairing with the codon is what matters.
